Overview

Tunis as a Business Centre

Tunis is the capital of Tunisia and the core of Greater Tunis, which takes in the governorates of Tunis, Ariana, Ben Arous and Manouba. According to reporting on Institut National de la Statistique (INS) figures, about 2.9 million people, roughly a quarter of the national population, live in Greater Tunis, and the 2024 census counted 1,075,306 residents in Tunis Governorate alone. The governorate hosts government offices, the stock exchange and the head offices of major businesses, and it is described as the country's largest industrial centre. Tunis-Carthage International Airport, a port with ferry links to Italy and France, and the country's main railway stations make the capital Tunisia's trade and transport hub.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Tunis because it is where Tunisian groups are headquartered, financed and litigated. A European manufacturer may rely on a supplier in the Greater Tunis industrial belt whose owners and related parties are not obvious from its correspondence. A lender or investor may deal with family-controlled groups spanning industry, distribution, finance and property. Counterparties in public contracts and regulated sectors often have links to officials in the capital, which raises questions of political exposure. When relationships fail, claims are pursued in the Tunis courts or through arbitration seated in the city, and counsel needs well-documented facts about the other side.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Tunis

01

Supplier ownership and integrity checks

Manufacturers and service providers across the Greater Tunis industrial belt supply European customers. We review registry extracts, published legal notices, litigation and Arabic and French media to establish who owns and manages a supplier, and to identify related parties, financial distress or reputational issues before contracts or acquisitions.

02

Family group and conglomerate mapping

Large Tunisian business groups headquartered in the capital combine industry, distribution, finance and property. We map shareholdings and directorships across group companies using registry data, stock exchange disclosures and media, showing how control is exercised and where related-party or politically exposed connections may arise.

03

Listed company and financial counterparties

Issuers on the Bourse de Tunis publish disclosures that are a valuable public source. We support compliance and investment teams reviewing listed companies, banks, leasing firms and intermediaries by examining ownership, published financial information, regulatory announcements and adverse media, together with the backgrounds of principals.

04

Public contract and PEP screening

Contracts and licences are awarded by ministries and public bodies in the capital. We research bidders, contractors and their owners for links to officials, prior awards, disputes and adverse media, distinguishing allegations from established findings, so clients can document enhanced due diligence on Tunis counterparties.

05

Litigation and arbitration fact support

Creditors and litigants in disputes with Tunis parties need to know what assets and related companies exist. We assemble corporate interests, media records and information obtained through Tunisian counsel to support proceedings in the Tunis courts or before the CCAT, with enforcement steps taken by local lawyers.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Tunis

Courts and award enforcement

Commercial disputes with Tunis companies are heard by the ordinary courts sitting in the capital. Tunisia does not have a separate commercial court, and business commentators have called for one, along with a mediation law, citing slow contract enforcement. Arbitral awards are enforced through the Court of Appeal, sometimes with certification by a first-instance judge, and enforcement can be refused on public order grounds or for serious procedural defects.

CCAT arbitration in Tunis

The Centre de Conciliation et d'Arbitrage de Tunis, founded in 1996, is described as the main arbitration institution in Tunisia. It administers conciliation and arbitration, provides hearing rooms and a library, and trains practitioners. Tunisia's Arbitration Code is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law. Investigative support for proceedings seated in Tunis is planned around the tribunal's procedural rules, confidentiality and the evidential standard counsel needs.

A planned CCI Tunis centre

In July 2026 the Chambre de Commerce et d'Industrie de Tunis launched a tender for an expert to design a conciliation, mediation and arbitration centre, relying on Law 2006-75 on chambers of commerce, with bids due on 7 August 2026. The project was at a preparatory stage when reported. Clients should check whether contracts with Tunis counterparties refer to this centre or to the CCAT.

Registry and records practice

Company information comes from the national Registre National des Entreprises, described on our Tunisia page, together with published legal notices and stock exchange disclosures for listed issuers. Because Tunis concentrates group headquarters, a single ownership question often spans companies registered across all four Greater Tunis governorates. Property and court searches are best made through Tunisian counsel, and certified Arabic translations are usually needed for court use.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Tunis

TDSC has no office in Tunis and works on Tunis matters from Nashville. We start by agreeing the purpose with the client and Tunisian counsel, whether supplier onboarding, a group ownership question, a listed or financial counterparty review, or support for litigation or CCAT arbitration. Research draws on registry extracts and legal notices, Bourse de Tunis disclosures, and Arabic and French media, supplemented by information obtained through counsel. We have not identified a licensing regime for private investigators in Tunisia, so any local inquiries are carried out by appropriate professionals engaged through counsel. Personal data is minimised and handled with Tunisia's data protection rules on transfers abroad in mind.

Questions

Tunis: Frequently Asked Questions

Can you identify the owners of a company based in Tunis?

Usually in large part. Registry extracts show legal form, capital, registered office and managers, and published legal notices record changes. Listed issuers publish further disclosures. Beneficial ownership data is not openly searchable, so we combine registry records, exchange filings, media and information obtained through Tunisian counsel, and we state clearly where control cannot be confirmed.

Is there a commercial court in Tunis?

Tunisia does not have a separate commercial court; commercial disputes go to the ordinary courts in the capital, and commentators have argued for a specialised court and a mediation law. Many commercial contracts instead provide for arbitration, often before the Centre de Conciliation et d'Arbitrage de Tunis. Counsel chooses the route; we supply the facts.

How are arbitral awards involving Tunis parties enforced?

Enforcement in Tunisia runs through the Court of Appeal, in some cases with certification by a first-instance judge, and may be refused for breach of public order or serious procedural errors. We help counsel prepare by identifying the debtor's companies, related parties and documented assets, so that enforcement steps can be targeted from the outset.

Are private investigators licensed in Tunisia?

We have not identified a statute licensing private investigators or detective agencies in Tunisia, and we do not assume that the activity is authorised as a profession. Covert surveillance and recording are constrained by data protection law. TDSC therefore scopes any local inquiries on Tunis matters with Tunisian counsel and engages appropriate professionals through them.

Do you work in Arabic and French for Tunis matters?

Yes. Registry notices, court documents and much of the press are in Arabic, while business correspondence and many corporate documents are in French. We review sources in both languages, report in English, and arrange certified translation through counsel where documents are needed for Tunisian courts or arbitral proceedings.
